The issue related to microcode in the Allen-Myland case was whether AMI’s unauthorized copying and adaptation of IBM’s 3090 mainframe microcode — to build a library of modified versions for reconfiguring and splitting customer systems — qualified as “an essential step in the utilization of the computer program” under Section 117(1) of the U.S. Copyright Act.

The court held that it did not. AMI’s copying was not for the purpose of executing the microcode on a machine as part of its intended use, but rather for creating a reusable library of modified microcode versions to be used across different systems. The court concluded that Section 117(1) permits copying only when it is an essential step in utilizing the program *in conjunction with a machine* — meaning, for execution — not for reverse engineering, adaptation, or redistribution. AMI’s actions, which involved making physical copies (on tape and hard disk) and maintaining them in a library for later use, were deemed outside the scope of the statutory exception.

The issue related to microcode in the Allen-Myland case was whether the unauthorized copying and adaptation of IBM’s 3090 mainframe microcode by Allen-Myland, Inc. (AMI) constituted a permissible “essential step in the utilization of the computer program” under Section 117(1) of the U.S. Copyright Act.
